analysis|06-20|1837|Η Βικτωρία ανεβαίνει στον θρόνο|Victoria Ascends the Throne|In 1837 King William IV died without surviving legitimate heirs, and the throne passed to his niece. Victoria was still a minor and the administration was unprepared for guidance. Political circles were anxious about the succession. The new queen was unknown to the wider public. The succession followed the procedure laid down by British law. // On 20 June 1837 the eighteen-year-old Victoria ascended the throne of Britain after the death of her uncle. The new queen gradually emerged as an important figure of her age. The beginning of her reign was accompanied by broad public sympathy. The public welcomed the new era with enthusiasm. Her uncle William IV had taken the throne in 1830. // Her reign lasted sixty-three years, the longest in British history up to that time. The age of Victoria became a symbol of the British Empire and of industrial progress. The queen was associated with the ideas of stability and duty. The term "Victorian era" is still used to describe that period. The queen was crowned in 1838, with a great ceremony in Westminster Abbey.

analysis|06-21|1788|Το Νιου Χάμσαϊρ επικυρώνει το Σύνταγμα|New Hampshire Ratifies the Constitution|The Constitution of the United States had been signed in 1787, but to come into force it required ratification by nine states. The disagreements were intense, with the Anti-Federalists demanding guarantees for the rights of citizens. The debate took place in each state separately. The process was difficult and uncertain. Ratification was carried out in a convention of each state separately. // On 21 June 1788 New Hampshire ratified the Constitution, becoming the ninth state to approve it. In this way the text passed the threshold required for it to take effect. Ratification was decisive for the course of the new system. The news quickly travelled to the other states. The Bill of Rights was adopted in 1791 as an addition to the Constitution. // This ratification opened the way for the implementation of the Constitution and for the first presidential elections. The rights eventually added to the Bill of Rights satisfied many of the objections. The history of ratification is regarded as critical for the shaping of American democracy. The event is a point of reference for constitutional history. George Washington was elected first president in 1789 by the unanimous vote of the electors.

analysis|06-21|1948|Τρέχει το πρώτο πρόγραμμα σε ηλεκτρονικό υπολογιστή|The First Program Runs on a Stored-Program Computer|After the Second World War researchers were seeking new ways of storing and processing information. The University of Manchester had a research group working on the development of electronic computers. The research had military and scientific applications. The capabilities of the machines were still limited. The team worked in university facilities with limited resources. // On 21 June 1948 the computer Manchester Baby ran its first program, which was stored in its memory. It was one of the first machines to operate on the stored-program model. The success of the test was important for the team. The result was published afterwards. The computer had a small memory system with bent cathode-ray tubes, known as the Williams tube. // This achievement was of great importance for the development of computers, and later machines were based on similar principles. Manchester is today recognised as one of the birthplaces of modern computing. The history of this computer is widely studied. The principle of the stored program is the foundation of modern systems. The program was short and showed the ability of the machine to solve mathematical problems.

analysis|06-22|1633|Ο Γαλιλαίος αναγκάζεται να αποκηρύξει τις απόψεις του|Galileo Is Forced to Recant|Galileo had supported the heliocentric system of Copernicus, which the Church regarded with suspicion. In 1616 he had received a warning not to teach the theory as proven. His relationship with Rome was strained. His scientific views provoked reactions. The trial continued with restrictions on his publications. // In 1632 he published the "Dialogue", and in 1633 he was brought before the Inquisition tribunal in Rome. On 22 June 1633 the tribunal obliged him to renounce his views on the motion of the Earth around the Sun. The trial was long and difficult for the scientist. The sentence was public. Galileo was condemned to house arrest, under strict supervision. // The trial of Galileo became a symbol of the clash between science and ecclesiastical authority. Galileo spent the last years of his life under house arrest. The affair left deep traces on the relationship between faith and science. His story is often cited as an example of the need for freedom of thought. The phrase "and yet it moves", attributed to him, is a later tradition and is not confirmed by the official documents.

analysis|06-22|1940|Ανακωχή της Γαλλίας με τη Γερμανία|Armistice between France and Germany|After the fall of Paris and the entry of the Germans into France, the Pétain government asked for an armistice. The German demands were harsh, and the French leadership considered that there was no other choice. The condition of the army was difficult. Public opinion was weary of the war. The armistice came into effect a few days later, with the agreement describing the division of the country. // On 22 June 1940 the armistice was signed at Compiègne, in the same railway carriage in which the German surrender had been signed in 1918. The choice of place was symbolic for the Germans, who wished to repay the humiliation of 1918. The agreement was reached under German insistence. The signing was highly symbolic. Pétain took office as head of the Vichy state on 10 July 1940. // The armistice led to the division of France into an occupied zone and a free zone, with the Vichy regime in the southern area. The agreement deeply affected the course of the war and the life of the French. The contradictions of the period are still discussed in the history of the country. The event remains central to the study of the French occupation. The railway carriage in which the signing took place had been moved to the same site, for the symbolic restoration of the 1918 signing.

analysis|06-22|1941|Η Γερμανία εισβάλλει στη Σοβιετική Ένωση|Germany invades the Soviet Union|In 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union had signed a non-aggression pact, with secret protocols for the division of Eastern Europe. The agreement remained in force for almost two years. The Soviet Union believed it would gain time for its defence. The preparation of the German attack was already under way. // On 22 June 1941 German forces launched Operation Barbarossa against the Soviet Union, on a huge front from the Baltic to the Black Sea. The attack was a surprise, with great initial successes. Soviet forces withdrew across much of the front. The conflict quickly developed into a war of annihilation. The invasion had been prepared for a long time, with large military forces concentrated on the eastern borders. // The invasion opened the largest front of the Second World War, with enormous losses on both sides. The battle remained in history as decisive for the outcome of the war in Europe. The analysis of the events continues to occupy historians. The operation marked the start of one of the harshest phases of the war. Stalin had ignored reports of the imminent attack, which historians still discuss.

analysis|06-23|1757|Η μάχη του Πλάσεϊ|The battle of Plassey|In the eighteenth century the East India Company expanded into Bengal, exploiting the weakness of the local rulers. The Company had its own military forces and sought commercial privileges. Clashes with the local rulers were frequent. The political situation of the region was unstable. The battle was fought with fewer soldiers on the side of the Company. // On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive, with the army of the Company, defeated the ruler of Bengal near Plassey, with the help of treacherous alliances. This victory opened the way to control of the region. The battle was short in comparison with its political result. The victors established a new administration. Clive's forces were fewer, but they had the advantage of the silent support of local leaders. // The battle of Plassey is regarded as the beginning of British rule in India, which continued for about two centuries. Its influence was deep in the economy, administration and society of the region. The history of the battle is examined today as part of colonial history. The event remains central to understanding India. With the victory, Clive took over the administration of Bengal on behalf of the Company.

analysis|06-23|1868|Πατεντάρεται η γραφομηχανή|The typewriter is patented|In the nineteenth century handwriting was slow, while the demand for clean and uniform documents was growing as offices, commercial enterprises and public services expanded. In this environment many inventors tried to make a machine that would print characters with keys, but the first attempts were imperfect. // Christopher Sholes, an American publisher and inventor, worked with a few friends in Milwaukee for years on the model. The system used keys that struck against an ink ribbon and paper, while the carriage moved after each character. On 23 June 1868 the invention was patented. // The typewriter changed the work of offices, since correspondence became faster and more legible, and the work of secretaries, in which many women found employment, entered a new era. The arrangement of the keys, known as QWERTY, was kept despite technological changes and is still used on computer keyboards. The patent gave the inventor legal protection so that he could commercially exploit the idea. The first machines were heavy and expensive, and the industry needed years to improve the mechanism and reduce the cost. Over time the typewriter became an indispensable tool of offices, lawyers, journalists and writers, and its development is connected with the history of education and administration.

analysis|06-23|1894|Ιδρύεται η Διεθνής Ολυμπιακή Επιτροπή|The International Olympic Committee is founded|At the end of the nineteenth century international sport was scattered among national events, and there was no common body to coordinate the competitions. The French educator Pierre de Coubertin believed that exercise could educate the young and bring peoples closer, and therefore proposed the revival of the ancient Olympic Games in modern form. // In June 1894, at a congress in Paris, representatives of several countries gathered. There the International Olympic Committee was founded, with the Greek scholar and politician Demetrios Vikelas as its first president, and it was decided that the first modern competition would take place in Athens. // The Committee became the centre of the modern Olympic movement, with responsibility for organising the Games and setting the rules of participation. The first modern Games took place in Athens in 1896, and Coubertin's idea became a worldwide institutional tradition that continues today. The founding of the Committee gave Olympism an institutional framework, with rules on the participation of athletes, on amateurism and on the choice of cities that would host the Games. The first Games of the modern era, in Athens in 1896, were based on this foundation, and the presence of athletes from several countries gave the event an international character. Since then the institution has developed considerably, with new sports, Winter Games and extensive television coverage.

analysis|06-24|1314|Η μάχη του Μπάνοκμπερν|The battle of Bannockburn|In the early fourteenth century Scotland resisted England's attempt to control the country, and Robert Bruce took the leadership of the resistance after 1306, when he was crowned king. The claim to the throne was at once a political and a national matter, and the war had become long, with alternating victories and defeats. // Near Bannockburn, outside Stirling, Bruce drew up his army in a position that made attack by the English forces difficult. In 1314 King Edward II attacked, but the English were defeated with heavy losses. The battle is regarded as the most important Scottish victory in the war of independence. // The victory did not immediately end the war, but it greatly strengthened Bruce's position, and he was eventually recognised as king. Scottish independence was formally recognised by treaty in 1328. The battle remained in Scottish memory as a symbol of national resistance. Bruce's victory also had political significance, since it strengthened the self-confidence of the Scottish nobles and of the common people who supported him. The course of the conflict showed that independence is not won by one battle alone but by lasting diplomacy and alliances, while Bruce's reign became a point of reference for Scottish national identity.

analysis|06-24|1812|Ο Ναπολέων περνά τον Νιέμεν|Napoleon crosses the Neman|In 1812 Napoleon had gathered a huge army from many European nations. The conflict with Russia arose from commercial disputes, since Tsar Alexander I did not observe the blockade system that the French emperor had imposed against Britain. Napoleon believed that a quick victory would impose his terms. // On 24 June 1812 the Grande Armée crossed the River Niemen and entered Russian territory. The Russians constantly withdrew and avoided a general battle, while the French struggled with the enormous distances, the heat, shortages of food and disease. // The campaign ended with the capture of Moscow and the painful retreat in winter, with enormous losses for the Grande Armée. The disaster weakened French hegemony in Europe and strengthened the alliances that led to Napoleon's fall a few years later. The invasion opened a war that exceeded all expectations, since the vast Russian space and the tactic of withdrawal made the French supply lines difficult. The experience of the campaign became a subject of study for the generals of the age, and it remains today a characteristic example of the dangers of a distant campaign without clear aims or secure supply lines.

analysis|06-24|1948|Αρχίζει ο αποκλεισμός του Βερολίνου|The Berlin Blockade begins|After the Second World War Germany and Berlin were divided into occupation zones among the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. The co-operation of the victors soon weakened, and Berlin, which lay within the Soviet zone, had western zones inside it. The currency reform in the western zones in June 1948 set off the crisis. // The Soviet Union responded by blocking the land routes, the rail lines and the roads to the western part of the city, with the aim of forcing it to give up the plans for the unification of the West. The Western powers did not withdraw, but organised an air bridge that carried food and fuel to the inhabitants. // The blockade ended in 1949, when the USSR lifted the restrictions without achieving its aim. The crisis accelerated the creation of NATO and the division of Germany into two states, and Berlin became a symbol of the Cold War. The air supply required the coordination of thousands of flights, with aircraft landing at the city's airports and carrying food, fuel and materials. This operation showed the Berliners that the West would not abandon them, and it contributed to shaping the political consciousness of the city for decades, while strengthening confidence in the Western powers.

analysis|06-25|1876|Η μάχη του Λιτλ Μπιγκχορν|The Battle of the Little Bighorn|In the 1870s the United States extended its power westward, and the peoples of the Plains continually lost their land. The discovery of gold in the Black Hills, an area sacred to the Lakota, and the violation of treaties led to resistance, which was strengthened by Cheyenne warriors and by other tribes. // In June 1876, near the Little Bighorn River in Montana, Colonel George Custer attacked a large encampment with a detachment of the 7th Cavalry. The strength of the indigenous forces had been underestimated, and Custer's detachment was divided, with the result that he himself and a large part of his men were killed. // Custer's death caused shock in the United States and led to a large escalation of the campaign by the federal forces. Shortly afterwards the tribes were forced to surrender, and their land was reduced by new agreements. The battle is often cited as a symbol of the tragic clash between expansion and the indigenous peoples. The success of the tribes did not change the fate of the war, since the government sent much larger forces and the campaign continued for several months. The battle remains in collective memory and in popular culture, and it is still today a subject of study for the history of the indigenous peoples of North America.

analysis|06-25|1910|Πρώτη παράσταση του «Πουλιού της Φωτιάς»|First performance of "The Firebird"|At the beginning of the twentieth century Paris was a centre of artistic innovation, and the company of the Ballets Russes of Sergei Diaghilev was looking for works that would surprise the audience. Igor Stravinsky was a young Russian composer who had no well-known name yet in the West, and he was commissioned to write the music for a ballet based on folk legends. // The premiere of "The Firebird" took place at the Paris Opera in June 1910, with choreography by Michel Fokine. The music was intensely rhythmic and coloured, with orchestral details that impressed the audience, and the performance attracted the attention of critics and artists. // The work opened the way for Stravinsky, who followed with other ballets such as "Petrushka" and "The Rite of Spring". Its success showed that ballet could combine modern music with tradition, and it deeply influenced the music and dance of the twentieth century. The ballet combined Russian folk elements with modern orchestral technique, and the collaboration of composer, choreographer and dancers gave a new form of theatrical expression. Its success opened the way for works that would change the history of music and ballet in the century that followed.

analysis|06-25|1950|Αρχίζει ο Πόλεμος της Κορέας|The Korean War begins|After the Second World War Korea was divided along the 38th parallel, with Soviet administration in the North and American administration in the South. The two zones acquired opposed regimes in 1948, and the division became permanent, while border clashes and threats of unification by force increased. // On 25 June 1950 the North Korean army crossed the parallel with large forces and quickly took Seoul. The UN Security Council condemned the invasion, and the United States together with other states, such as Britain, sent troops under the flag of the Organisation, while China later sided with North Korea. // The war lasted three years and cost the lives of millions of people, civilians and soldiers. It ended with an armistice in 1953, without a formal peace treaty, and Korea remains divided. The war shaped the perception of the Cold War in Asia. The conflict was strongly internationalised, because the superpowers of the period supported opposing sides, and the war became a reference point for Cold War strategy. The losses among the civilian population were particularly great, and the destruction of the cities left an indelible mark on the society of the peninsula.

analysis|06-25|1975|Η Μοζαμβίκη γίνεται ανεξάρτητη|Mozambique becomes independent|Mozambique had been a Portuguese colony for centuries, and in the 1960s and 1970s the anti-colonial organisation FRELIMO fought for independence. The overthrow of the regime in Lisbon in 1974 opened the way to negotiations, and Portugal decided to grant independence to its colonies. // On 25 June 1975 Mozambique was proclaimed independent, with Samora Machel, the leader of FRELIMO, as its first president. The transition was rapid, since the administrative and economic machinery of the colony had been largely abandoned and many Portuguese had left the country. // The new government followed a socialist policy and soon came into conflict with opponents, which led to a civil war that lasted until the early 1990s. The war left deep wounds, but independence remained a landmark for African liberation from colonialism. The liberation process brought to power a party with long anti-colonial experience, which tried to organise the economy and education in a state that had very few local technicians and administrators. These difficulties increased the tensions, and the period was decisive for the country's later course.

analysis|06-25|1991|Ανεξαρτησία της Σλοβενίας και της Κροατίας|Independence of Slovenia and Croatia|After the death of Tito, in the 1980s, Yugoslavia faced an economic crisis and intense national tensions among its republics. Slovenia and Croatia, more prosperous and with a strong desire for autonomy, demanded greater self-government, while the Serbian leadership strengthened central power. // On 25 June 1991 the parliaments of the two republics declared their independence. The federal government and the army reacted, and in Slovenia the conflict was brief, lasting around ten days. In Croatia violence escalated, as Serb communities rebelled and fighting intensified. // The dissolution of Yugoslavia led to a series of wars, in Croatia, in Bosnia and later in Kosovo. Slovenia completed its independence with fewer losses and later joined the European Union, while the other wars left deep traumas. The process is one of the most important events of the Balkans after the Cold War. The recognition of the two states by the European Community came a few months later, and international recognition was linked with the negotiations for peace in the region. This process changed the map of the Balkans, and the history of the dissolution of Yugoslavia remains a subject of study for the history of Europe.

analysis|06-26|363|Πεθαίνει ο αυτοκράτορας Ιουλιανός|Emperor Julian dies|At the end of the fourth century the Roman Empire faced continual wars with the Persians, and Emperor Julian, who had tried to revive pagan worship, wanted to demonstrate the military power of the state. The campaign in Persia seemed an opportunity for a decisive victory. // In the summer of 363 the army penetrated deep into Persian territory, but the Persians refused a general battle and applied a tactic of attrition. During a skirmish Julian was mortally wounded and died shortly afterwards. The sources differ in their details, so certainty should be avoided. // The generals elected Jovian as successor, who made peace with the Persians and ceded territories. The campaign ended without victory, and the death of Julian put an end to the attempt to revive the old religion. His reign remains in history as short but significant, because it revealed the limits of Roman power. His brief reign left a figure who has been much discussed by contemporaries and later historians, since it combined philosophical learning, religious reform and political ambition. His death marked the end of the plan to restore pagan worship, and the Church gained ground in the years that followed, while the empire turned to a more conservative course.

analysis|06-26|1945|Υπογράφεται ο Χάρτης των Ηνωμένων Εθνών|The Charter of the United Nations is signed|World War II had shown that the League of Nations could not prevent conflict, and the great powers of the alliance wanted to create a new organisation with stronger mechanisms. In the negotiations at Dumbarton Oaks and at Yalta the basic principles had already been determined. // In the summer of 1945 a conference with delegates from many states met in San Francisco, which completed the text of the Charter. On 26 June representatives of fifty states signed it, and the Charter defined the organs of the Organisation and the powers of the Security Council. // The United Nations was officially founded in October, when the Charter was ratified by the required states. The founding marked a new effort for international peace and security, and since then the Organisation has dealt with humanitarian aid, the settlement of disputes and peacekeeping missions, although its effectiveness has often been questioned. The Charter states that the Organisation's aims are the maintenance of international peace, the development of friendly relations among states and the promotion of human rights. The privilege of the great powers, with the veto in the Security Council, became a matter of discussion from the beginning, but the Charter remained the foundation of the international order after the war.

analysis|06-26|1960|Η Μαδαγασκάρη ανεξαρτητοποιείται|Madagascar becomes independent|After the Second World War Madagascar was a French colony, and anti-colonial activity had grown strong after the uprising of 1947, which was violently suppressed. Malagasy politicians began to claim greater autonomy, and France was forced to consider the question of independence. // Negotiations led to the recognition of independence, and on 26 June 1960 France recognised the island as an independent country. The first president of the new republic was Philibert Tsiranana, one of the main politicians of the period. // Independence opened the way to complex relations with France, which maintained economic and cultural ties with the new country. The political developments of the following decades showed that the separation from colonialism did not always mean stability, but the event remained important for the history of the island. The independence of the island was not only a political act but also the result of a long process of negotiations, during which the French administration tried to preserve its influence. The national identity of the Malagasy, with the many ethnic groups of the island, became a basic element of the new political organisation of the state. The transition to independence left questions about economic dependence on France, which remained strong for many years.

analysis|06-26|1963|«Ich bin ein Berliner»|Ich bin ein Berliner|In 1963 Berlin was still divided, and the Wall built in 1961 was a symbol of the Cold War. The western city lived with a sense of isolation, and its inhabitants worried whether the West would defend them at the critical moment. // On 26 June 1963 the American president John F. Kennedy spoke to a crowd in West Berlin and used the phrase "Ich bin ein Berliner", meaning that he too is a Berliner. The statement caused great enthusiasm and was a clear message to the Soviet Union. // The speech strengthened the image of the United States as the guarantor of the security of the West and became one of the best-known political messages of the twentieth century. The phrase shows how important the city was in the confrontation of the two blocs, and it is still repeated as a symbol of solidarity. Kennedy's phrase had been carefully prepared, and his speech was recognised as a declaration of support for a city living under pressure. The Berliners welcomed the president with great enthusiasm, and the speech remained in history as one of the most famous political messages of the Cold War, with consequences for western policy in Germany.

analysis|06-27|1954|Λειτουργεί ο πρώτος πυρηνικός σταθμός|The first nuclear power plant begins operating|After the Second World War the Soviet Union invested in nuclear research, at first for military purposes and soon also for the civil use of atomic energy. Scientists wanted to show that atomic energy could produce electricity safely for citizens. // On 27 June 1954 the nuclear reactor at Obninsk, near Moscow, supplied an electricity grid for the first time. The installation is regarded as the first nuclear power station to generate electricity for common use, despite its small size. // The success at Obninsk opened the way to the development of nuclear energy in many countries, with different models and technologies. The event was a milestone for nuclear technology, but safety and waste management later became key issues in public debate. The Obninsk reactor had a small capacity, but its operation proved that nuclear energy could be linked to an electricity distribution network. The experience helped in the design of later plants, and nuclear technology became part of the energy policy of many countries in the following decades. The experience of Obninsk contributed to the development of the reactors that were later used in many countries of the world.

analysis|06-27|1977|Το Τζιμπουτί ανεξαρτητοποιείται|Djibouti becomes independent|France had for decades held the region of East Africa known as French Somaliland or the French Afars and Issas. The dispute between those who wanted union with neighbouring states and those who preferred to keep their ties with France influenced the politics of the region for years. // In 1977, after a referendum, the territory was proclaimed independent under the name Djibouti, on 27 June. The first president was Hassan Gouled Aptidon, who led the country for many years. The transition took place peacefully, without great violence. // Djibouti gained value as a strategic port, close to the sea passages that link the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. The French presence was maintained through a military base, and the country became an example of the complexity of decolonisation in small states with strong external relations. The French presence in the area was of strategic importance for the West, since the port of the Red Sea controls much of the sea traffic towards Suez. Independence did not immediately resolve the ethnic and political differences, but Djibouti maintained relative stability in an area with many tensions. The region continues to have particular geopolitical importance for the sea routes of the area.

analysis|06-28|1914|Η δολοφονία στο Σεράγεβο|The assassination in Sarajevo|On 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo in Bosnia, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, visited the city. The visit had something of the significance of a provocation, since the day was the anniversary of the battle of Kosovo and Bosnia had been annexed by Austria-Hungary a few years earlier. Tensions with Serbia were already high. // A young Bosnian Serb, Gavrilo Princip, who was connected with a nationalist circle, fired at the couple's car and killed Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie. The incident shocked Europe and led to diplomatic reactions that quickly escalated. // The assassination became the pretext for Austro-Hungarian demands on Serbia, which were linked with the system of alliances of the period. Within a few weeks Europe was at war in the First World War. The event remains as the critical point that turned a local crisis into a European conflict. The reaction in Vienna and Berlin strongly influenced the course of the crisis, since the Austro-Hungarian government believed it could punish Serbia without provoking a wider conflict. These calculations proved wrong, and the event remains an example of how a local murder can overturn a whole diplomatic balance.

analysis|06-28|1914|Δολοφονείται ο αρχιδούκας Φραγκίσκος Φερδινάνδος|Archduke Franz Ferdinand is assassinated|On 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo in Bosnia, Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were shot by the young Gavrilo Princip, a member of a nationalist circle. Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia a few years earlier, something that irritated Serbia and the nationalists of the region. // The attack took place during the official visit of the couple to the city, and the couple were killed. The Austro-Hungarian government considered that Serbia was responsible, and so a diplomatic escalation began that was fed by the promises of the allies. // Within a few weeks the event led to a war that spread across Europe. The assassination was not the only cause of the war, but it was the pretext that opened the way to a conflict-ridden world, with consequences that lasted for decades. The murder of the couple caused a wave of emotion and anger in Austro-Hungarian society, and the government exploited the incident to pursue a harsh policy towards Serbia. The memory of the event remains intense, and Sarajevo became a symbol of the beginning of the war that marked the twentieth century. The link of the event with the alliances of the period made the war almost inevitable within a few weeks.

analysis|06-28|1919|Υπογράφεται η Συνθήκη των Βερσαλλιών|The Treaty of Versailles is signed|After the First World War Europe was exhausted, and the victors wanted to impose their terms on Germany. The negotiations in Paris lasted for months, and the views of the great powers on reparations and territory differed greatly. // On 28 June 1919, in the Palace of Versailles, the treaty with Germany was signed, in the presence of representatives of the victors. Germany was forced to accept responsibility for the war, to limit its army and to pay reparations. // The treaty remained in history as a cause of resentment in Germany and contributed to the climate that allowed the rise of National Socialism. At the same time it set the borders of Europe and supported the creation of the League of Nations, which dominated international relations between the wars. The treaty also included the establishment of the League of Nations, which was regarded as the main mechanism for peace, although the United States did not ratify it. The contrast between the terms of the treaty and the expectations of the Germans contributed to a climate of intense resentment that affected the country's politics in the following years. The decisions on borders and reparations are still discussed by historians and diplomats today.

analysis|06-29|1613|Καίγεται το θέατρο Globe|The Globe Theatre burns down|In the seventeenth century the Globe Theatre in London was one of the most important venues for theatrical performances, and the plays of Shakespeare were staged there by his company. The performances often used effects and gunshots to impress the audience. // On 29 June 1613, during a performance of "Henry VIII", a cannon used for the effects set fire to the thatched roof, and the fire spread rapidly and destroyed the building within a few hours. // The theatre was rebuilt the following year, with a tiled roof, and continued to operate as an important venue of the English stage. The episode shows the dangers of the old theatres, and at the same time testifies to the importance of the Globe for the cultural life of London in the age of the Tudors and the Stuarts. The fire was one of the most significant events in the history of the English theatre, since many plays of Shakespeare had been staged on its stage. The theatrical companies of the period soon returned to work, and the rebuilding showed the importance of the theatre for the cultural life of London. The history of the theatre is linked with the development of the drama of the period and with the presence of the greatest writers of London.

analysis|06-29|1976|Οι Σεϋχέλλες ανεξαρτητοποιούνται|Seychelles becomes independent|The Seychelles had been a British possession since the early nineteenth century, and the island economy relied on plantations and on a tourism that was only beginning. In the 1960s the growing autonomy of the colonies of the Indian Ocean brought the question of independence to the fore. // On 29 June 1976 the Seychelles officially became an independent state within the Commonwealth, with James Mancham as its first president. The transition took place smoothly, without serious conflict, and the new state inherited the language and institutions of Britain. // Independence did not bring stability immediately, as shortly afterwards the political scene changed through a coup. The country became known as a small state with strong tourism, and its relations with Western countries were maintained largely through economic and military ties. Independence was linked with the need for economic diversification, since agriculture and fishing were not enough for a small society living on remote islands.
